description: The device-pairing contract, shared by every client. This file is the ONE owner of the connection-phase names, the WebSocket policy-close code the gateway uses for a pairing rejection, the rules that read that close into a pairing state (and pull the requestId out of the reason), the plain-language copy a client shows, and the injected script that observes the page's own gateway socket and reports the pairing close to the native layer. core/pairing.js reads it (the desktop reads that module, core/test asserts it against core/fixtures/pairing.json); the iOS client bundles THIS FILE and ports the parser as constants, proving the port against the same fixtures, and installs the observer through a WKUserScript so there is one copy of the script in the tree rather than one per client.
why: The gateway holds a second gate after auth: device pairing. A client that passed the token check but is not an approved device is refused at the socket, with WebSocket close code 1008 (Policy Violation) and a reason of the shape `pairing required: <requirement> (requestId: <id>)`. This is a DIFFERENT state from an auth failure (a bad or missing token) and from a network drop (the socket never opened, or dropped without a policy reason): each has different messaging and a different recovery, so the parse below keeps them apart deliberately and a client must not collapse them.

The mobile client hosts the Control UI in a web view, and the PAGE opens the gateway socket, so the pairing close is an event inside the page rather than a native navigation failure: the page's HTML loaded fine, so `didFinishNavigation` already fired and the native layer thinks it connected. The only way the native layer learns the socket was refused for pairing is to observe the page's own WebSocket. The observer script here does exactly that and nothing else: it watches `close`, and when the code and reason say pairing it posts the parsed state out. It does not touch `send`, does not read a credential, and reports only the three fields a pairing screen needs.

The requestId is what the operator matches when they approve, and it travels in the close REASON string rather than in a structured detail object, because a raw WebSocket close carries only a numeric code and a short reason string. So the parser's job is string parsing, held to a strict id pattern so a malformed reason cannot inject arbitrary text into a screen. The id pattern and the `(requestId: <id>)` shape mirror the gateway's own `connect-error-details` contract in the OpenClaw checkout (packages/gateway-protocol/src/connect-error-details.ts), so the two agree by construction rather than by luck.

The reason strings the gateway emits are matched by the same substrings the gateway's own reader uses: `pairing required` for the first-connection case, and the upgrade phrasings for the three upgrade reasons. A close that is code 1008 but whose reason is NOT a pairing reason is left as an ordinary failure, because 1008 is a general policy code and not pairing's alone.

The copy lives here so both clients say the same thing, and it reflects the REAL instruction the gateway and the Control UI give (`openclaw devices approve <requestId>`, or `openclaw devices approve --latest` when there is no id), rather than an invented one. The command is shown for the operator to run on the gateway host; the client cannot run it, and says so.

`timing` is here for the same one-owner reason, and it is the one part of the screen that is a cadence rather than a string. Both clients keep the pairing screen up while they wait for an approval, and both must reissue a connect attempt on a sane interval (`retrySeconds`) and take the screen down only once an open has SURVIVED a short settle window (`confirmSeconds`). Two clients with two copies of those numbers drift the first time one is tuned, and the visible symptom is one client flickering where the other does not, so they live here and both read them: core/pairing.js exports them, the Swift port reads them off the bundled spec. The values are a balance, documented where they are used: long enough not to hammer a gateway that is deliberately refusing this device and to outlast the gap between a socket open and the 1008 close that follows it, short enough that an operator's approval reaches the user promptly.

It is an ARRAY of lines for the script, not one escaped string, for the same reason prompt-metadata's hook is: a maintainable escape is the only kind that survives an edit, each line reads as a line, and the readers join with a newline.

`socketClosed` is the observer's OTHER report, and the reason it belongs in the same script: the observer already watches the page's own WebSocket, and a socket that HAD opened and has now closed without a pairing reason is this client's session ending. Nothing else can see that. The page loaded fine, so a navigation-level failure never fires, and the client would go on presenting a gateway page that looks authenticated while nothing is connected, which is a worse state than a missing screen: it tells the reader something untrue about whether they are connected, in the one place they would look to find out. So the client stops presenting that view and shows its own surface instead.

A close from a socket that never opened is deliberately NOT this report. A handshake that never completed is not a session ending, and the commonest one is a token the gateway refused, where the page's own login gate is the thing the reader needs on screen. So the observer only reports a close for a socket it saw OPEN, and a client that receives this for a socket it never watched open is receiving something the contract does not promise.

★ ONE SESSION SOCKET, because the page opens others and they are not this client's connection. Measured 2026-09-17, from a report of two symptoms together: refreshing the Control UI's browser side panel made the main UI refresh, and closing it left the whole app stuck on the client's own failure surface, showing the gateway address and a Try again button, while the page's gateway socket was open and healthy the whole time. One cause, and it was OURS rather than the page's: the observer wrapped EVERY WebSocket and posted `disconnected` for ANY of them that had opened and then closed, so the browser panel putting its own screencast stream down was reported as this client's session ending. The shipped panel builds that socket itself (dist/control-ui/assets/browser-panel-*.js, one WebSocket at the `wsPath` the gateway hands it), so its close arrives in exactly the shape this report looks for: a socket that opened, and no pairing reason. The two symptoms are the two halves of the one misreading. CLOSING the panel raised the shell's failure surface, and then nothing opened a socket again, which is why only the reader's Try again took it down. REFRESHING it closed that socket and immediately opened another, and the open was reported as the device authenticating, which sent the shell through its own reconnect and reloaded the Control UI under the reader. What ruled the other explanations out: the panel is a dock inside the Control UI's OWN document, not a view, a partition or a webContents of its own, so there is no second view whose reload could reload the first, and the view holding the main page is only ever replaced by a connect attempt, which no panel action reaches. So the fix is here rather than in a client: the report is about the page's SESSION socket, which is the FIRST socket it opens, because a panel's stream cannot be opened before the page has authenticated, its path coming back from an authenticated request. A session socket that closes releases the name, so the page's own reconnect takes it, TO THE SAME ENDPOINT, and that qualifier is the second half of this fix rather than a detail. Releasing the name to ANY socket was measured the same day to still reproduce the report: after a session close the next socket the page opens is likelier to be a feature than the session, a browser panel opened or refreshed while the app holds its failure surface, and its open was posted as the device authenticating, which is the report that re-runs the app's own load path, so a PANEL action reloaded the main view under the reader and wiped what they had typed. So the endpoint the session socket was opened at is remembered, and a later socket is adopted only when it is at the same host and path; a feature socket is opened at its own path (the browser stream, an audio session, a desktop panel), and the query is deliberately not compared so a token or cache-buster cannot break the page's own reconnect. Uncomparable endpoints still adopt, which is the behaviour this had, because losing the page's own reconnect would leave the reader on the failure surface for good and that is the worse of the two. Those bytes are the same on both clients, so the phone is fixed with the desktop. The residual assumption, stated because being wrong would name the wrong socket: a page whose first socket is NOT its session would be misread, and the place to correct that is here.

`routing` is here because WHICH state a pairing close puts the reader in depends on where it arrived: a first connection is a setup problem and the pairing screen is the whole answer, while the same close arriving at a session that was already approved and working is a REVOCATION, and that reader needs the settings surface with the gateway row saying the device needs approval, because the first thing to check is which gateway this client is even pointed at. Two clients deciding that separately would drift into two behaviours for one event, so the rule and the surface names live here and both clients route through `pairingRoute()` in core/pairing.js.

requirements.not-paired: This device is not approved yet.
requirements.role-upgrade: This device is asking for a higher role than was approved.
requirements.scope-upgrade: This device is asking for more access than was approved.
requirements.metadata-upgrade: This device changed and must be approved again.

copy.title: Approve this device
copy.body: This device reached the gateway, but the gateway has not approved it yet. Approve it on the gateway host and this screen clears on its own.
copy.commandLabel: Run this on the gateway host
copy.waiting: Waiting for approval. This connects on its own once the request is approved.
copy.cannotRunHere: This device cannot approve itself; the command runs on the gateway host.

hook: if (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(SUBSTRINGS, key) && text.indexOf(SUBSTRINGS[key]) !== -1) { found = key; break; }
var requestId = match && ID_PATTERN.test(match[1]) ? match[1] : null;
// THE PAGE'S OWN GATEWAY SOCKET, which is the FIRST socket it opens. Every
// other socket the page opens belongs to a feature rather than to this
// client's session: the browser panel's screencast stream, a terminal, an
// audio session. A close from one of those is not this connection ending,
// and an open from one is not this device authenticating. See the why entry
// The endpoint the page's OWN gateway socket was opened at, remembered so a
// LATER socket can only take the session over if it is that same endpoint
// coming back. Measured 2026-09-17: releasing the name on close alone let the
// NEXT socket to open be adopted, and after any session close the next socket to
// open is likelier to be a feature than the session, a browser panel being
// opened or refreshed while the app holds its failure surface. Its open was
// posted as the device authenticating, which is the report that re-runs the
// app's own load path, so a PANEL action reloaded the main view under the
// reader and wiped what they had typed. Host and path only, never the query: a
// token or cache-buster must not break the page's own reconnect, and a feature
// socket is a different path (the browser stream, an audio session, a panel).
var socket = protocols === undefined ? new OpenSocket(url) : new OpenSocket(url, protocols);
if (pairing) { post({ kind: 'pairing-required', reason: pairing.reason, requestId: pairing.requestId }); return; }
// Reported once, and the name is released so the page's own reconnect to
// the SAME endpoint can take it: a socket that has closed is not the session
// any more, and neither is any other socket the page happens to open.
// A socket at another endpoint is a feature, not this connection: its
// open must not be reported as the device authenticating. Uncomparable
// endpoints fall through to adopting, which is the behaviour this had,
// because losing the page's own reconnect would leave the reader on the
// failure surface for good and that is the worse of the two.
if (sessionEndpoint !== null && endpoint !== null && endpoint !== sessionEndpoint) return;
